A simplified proof of polynomial improvements for 3SUM and APSP

**Abstract**

We give a simplified proof of the polynomial improvements for integer 3SUM and all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) established by Alman and Vassilevska Williams, with weaker exponents. The central ingredient is selected-entry matrix multiplication: computing a prescribed set of entries of a product of dense rectangular matrices. Starting from Schönhage’s inner/outer- product identity, we construct a multiplication rule that shares intermediate products among many outputs. We apply this rule recursively and bound the work by counting the requested entries at each level.

Applied to incidence matrices, the algorithm solves Offline Set Disjointness over a small universe. Known deterministic reductions then yield truly subquadratic integer 3SUM and truly subcubic APSP for polynomially bounded integer inputs.

## 1 Introduction

Alman and Vassilevska Williams [1] established the first truly subquadratic algorithms for integer 3SUM and truly subcubic algorithms for all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer inputs. Their main innovation is a matrix multiplication algorithm that exploits sparsity in the set of requested outputs, even when the input matrices are dense. We give a simplified proof of these qualitative improvements, with weaker exponents.

We focus on the matrix multiplication argument. To obtain the 3SUM and APSP consequences, we first apply it to Offline Set Disjointness, where matrix entries directly encode intersection sizes. We then use existing deterministic reductions from 3SUM and APSP to this problem as black boxes.

Selected-entry matrix multiplication. Let _X_ be an \(n\times d\) matrix and _Y_ a \(d\times m\) matrix. Each entry of _XY_ is a dot product of a row of _X_ and a column of _Y_ . We call the task of computing _w_ specified entries of _XY selected-entry matrix multiplication_. Computing these entries as separate dot products uses _wd_ multiplications, while writing down the full product takes \(\Omega(nm)\) time. When the middle dimension _d_ and the number of requested entries _w_ are small enough, sharing intermediate computations gives the following bound.

**Theorem 1.1** (Selected-entry matrix multiplication)**.** _For every fixed_ \(\tau\in(0,1]\)_, there is an integer_ \(\kappa=\kappa(\tau)=O(\tau^{-2})\) _with the following property. Let_ \(d^\kappa\le min\{n,m\}\)_. Given integer matrices_ \(X\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times d}\) _and_ \(Y\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times m}\)_, with entries of polynomial magnitude in n+m, and_ \(w\ge 1\) _distinct specified positions in XY, those entries can be computed deterministically in time_

\(\widetilde{O}((n+m)d^\kappa+d^\tau\sqrt{nmw}).\) (1)

The first term pays for preparing linear combinations of the inputs; the second pays for multiplying these forms and reconstructing the requested outputs. Reducing \(\tau\) makes the latter cheaper, at the expense of increasing \(\kappa\) and restricting the allowable middle dimension _d_. Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\] call such products _thin_ and the prescribed outputs _wanted entries_.

For example, take \(\tau=1/4\), let \(\kappa=\kappa(1/4)\), and suppose \(d^{\kappa+1}\le n\). Computing \(w=\lfloor n^2/d\rfloor\) specified entries of an \(n\times d\) by \(d\times n\) product then takes \(\widetilde{O}(n^2/d^{1/4})\) time. Separate dot products would take \(\Theta(n^2)\) operations, and the full product has _n_<sup>2</sup> entries. When _d_ is a fixed positive power of _n_, this saves a polynomial factor over both approaches.

### Fine grained algorithms.

Integer 3SUM asks whether a list of _n_ integers contains three entries with distinct indices whose sum is zero. All-pairs shortest paths (APSP) asks for the shortest-path distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a directed graph. We allow negative edge weights but assume there is no negative cycle. Combining Theorem 1.1 with known reductions gives the following corollary.

**Corollary 1.2.** _There are absolute constants_ \(\delta_1,\delta_2>0\) _such that integer 3SUM on n polynomially bounded integers has a deterministic_ \(O(n^{2-\delta_1})\)_-time algorithm, and APSP on an n-vertex directed graph with polynomially bounded integer edge weights and no negative cycle has a deterministic_ \(O(n^{3-\delta_2})\)_-time algorithm._

We have not tried to optimize the constants; our focus is on simplicity of exposition.

## 1.1 Proof overview

### Selected-entry matrix multiplication.

The algebraic starting point is the inner/outer-product identity of Schönhage \[2\], used by Coppersmith \[3\] for rectangular matrix multiplication. Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\] adapt this approach to exploit the overlap among the computations needed by selected entries. We express this sharing through an exact multiplication rule: each output is a sum of six products from a common collection, minus one private correction term. The common collection is small relative to the number of outputs, and the same intermediate value can serve many requested entries. We apply the rule recursively to matrix blocks and count the resulting requests, capping each count by the number of available output positions. Our simplification is in the explicit rule and this counting argument; the central idea of exploiting sparse output requests comes from Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\].

### Fine grained algorithms.

In _Offline Set Disjointness_ \[4, 5\], we are given two families of sets and a list of pairs, one set from each family, and must determine which pairs are disjoint. The product of the families’ incidence matrices records all intersection sizes. When the universe is small, Theorem 1.1 computes the requested intersection sizes efficiently. For 3SUM, we use the direct deterministic reduction of Fischer, Kaliciak, and Polak \[5\]. For APSP, we use the standard reduction to Exact Triangle, followed by the deterministic reduction to lopsided triangle queries of Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\].

### Further research.

How far can selected-entry matrix multiplication be improved? What is the best possible dependence on the middle dimension _d_ when computing _w_ arbitrary entries of an \(n\times d\) by \(d\times n\) product? Can we reduce the \(d^\tau\) loss in Theorem 1.1 without increasing the input-preparation cost or requiring thinner matrices? Can comparable savings hold for larger _d_? For which ranges of _d_ and _w_ can selected-entry algorithms substantially outperform the best rectangular<tbc>

matrix multiplication algorithms for computing the full product? It would also be valuable to find simpler multiplication rules or entirely different algorithms achieving such savings. Progress on these questions may also lead to stronger algorithms for 3SUM, APSP, and other fine grained algorithmic problems.

### AI methodology.

Agentin AI coordinated a large research swarm of AI agents to explore alternative proof strategies and candidate simplifications, contributing to the development of the simplified proof presented here. The authors directed the mathematical investigation, critically evaluated the proposed arguments, and developed and refined the proof and exposition through iterative work with ChatGPT and x. This process included checking calculations, simplifying the recursive analysis, separating input-preparation costs from multiplication costs, and improving the presentation. The authors take responsibility for the final manuscript.

### Acknowledgements.

We thank Virginia Vassilevska Williams for helpful comments.

### Organization.

After brief preliminaries, Section 2 proves the selected-entry bound, and Section 3 applies it to set disjointness and derives the 3SUM and APSP consequences using known reductions.

### Preliminaries.

Throughout, \[_t_\]={1_,...,t_} and logarithms have base two. We write \(\widetilde{O}(f)\) for _O(f_) up to polylogarithmic factors. All integer inputs are polynomially bounded in the relevant size parameter, so they have logarithmic bit length. Arithmetic on such integers costs only polylogarithmic time, which is absorbed by \(\widetilde{O}\).

## 2 Selected-entry matrix multiplication

Theorem 1.1 follows from the main theorem, which gives a more precise bound on the runtime of the selected-entry matrix multiplication algorithm.

**Theorem 2.1** (Combinatorial bound)**.** _Fix an integer_ \(k\ge 81\)_. Let_ \(d^{6k}\le min\{n,m\}\) _and_ \(t=\lceil log_2d\rceil\)_. Given integer matrices_ \(X\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times d}\) _and_ \(Y\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times m}\) _with entries of polynomial magnitude in n+m, any_ \(w\ge 1\) _distinct specified entries of XY can be computed deterministically in time_

\(\widetilde{O}\left((n+m)d^{6k}+\sum_{s=0}^t\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t}{s}6^smin\left\{w,\frac{nm}{k^s}\right\}\right).\) (2)

The following convenient corollary simplifies the runtime in terms of a single parameter \(\theta\in[0,1]\).

**Corollary 2.2** (Density tradeoff)**.** _Under the assumptions of Theorem 2.1, the same algorithm runs in time_<tbc>

\(\widetilde{O}\left((n+m)d^{6k}+(nm)^\theta w^{1-\theta} d^{log_2(1+6/k^\theta)}\right)(0\le\theta\le 1).\) (3)

<tbc>_Proof._ Using \(min\{x,y\}\le x^{1-\theta} y^\theta\) and the binomial theorem,

\(\sum_{s=0}^t\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t}{s}6^smin\left\{w,\frac{nm}{k^s}\right\}\le(nm)^\theta w^{1-\theta}\sum_{s=0}^t\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t}{s}(6/k^\theta)^s=(nm)^\theta w^{1-\theta}(1+6/k^\theta)^t.\)

Since \(t=\lceil log_2d\rceil\), the last factor is \(O(d^{log_2(1+6/k^\theta)})\).

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ Take \(k=\lceil 81/\tau^2\rceil\) and \(\kappa=6k\). Then \(1+6/\sqrt{k}\le 1+2\tau/3<2^\tau\), so Theorem 2.2 with \(\theta=1/2\) gives the claim.

We prove Theorem 2.1 in the remainder of this section.

### Proof idea.

We first construct a small matrix multiplication rule in which outputs use six products from the same shared collection minus one private product per output. We apply this rule recursively to blocks of larger matrices, following only the intermediate entries needed for the requested outputs. We count these requests by their pattern of private and shared steps. Each shared step generates at most six requests per incoming request, but the count is capped by the total number of output positions in the corresponding products. The base case is an outer product, whose requested entries each require one multiplication. Padding the input dimensions lets us apply this count directly to the given matrices.

## 2.1 The multiplication rule

For a matrix product _UV_ , call _U_ the left input and _V_ the right input. A _product of linear forms_ multiplies an integer linear combination of entries of _U_ by an integer linear combination of entries of _V_ . We count the additions and subtractions needed to form these combinations separately from their multiplication.

**Lemma 2.3** (A shared multiplication rule)**.** _Let_ \(k\ge 2\) _and set R=k_2<sup>_k_-1</sup> _and S_=3<sup>_k_-1</sup>_. We construct a multiplication rule for matrices_ \(U\in\mathbb{Z}^{R\times 2}\) _and_ \(V\in\mathbb{Z}^{2\times S}\) _as follows:_

1. **_Products:_** _There is a common collection of_ 6_<sup>k</sup>_ shared _products and one_ private _product for each entry of UV_.<tbc>

2. **_Linear forms:_** _Every product multiplies a linear form in U by a linear form in V. Each form is a sum of at most_ 6_k signed entries of its respective matrix._<tbc>

_3._ **_Reconstruction:_** _Each entry of UV is the sum of six shared products minus its private product._

We count products by their labels, even if two formulas happen to be identical. The multiplication has _RS=k_6<sup>_k_-1</sup> outputs, but only 6_<sup>k</sup>_ shared products. Thus

\(\frac{\text{number of shared products}}{\text{number of outputs}}=\frac{6^k}{RS}=\frac{6}{k}.\)

As _k_ increases, the shared collection becomes small relative to the number of outputs. This is the reuse that our recursive algorithm will exploit.

### A cancellation identity.

The construction follows the Schönhage-Coppersmith approach used by Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\]. We first give a cancellation identity, then construct shared linear forms whose restriction to each output has exactly this pattern. The identity is the \(2\times 3\) instance of Schönhage’s inner/outer-product cancellation \[2\].

For the desired dot product _p_<sub>1</sub>_q_<sub>1</sub>+_p_<sub>2</sub>_q_<sub>2</sub>, we add a third coordinate with _p_<sub>3</sub>=0 and _q_<sub>3</sub>=-_q_<sub>1</sub>-_q_<sub>2</sub>. The first relation preserves the dot product, while the zero sum of the _q<sub>j</sub>_ cancels a mixed term. The remaining unwanted terms are removed by one private product. Figure 1 illustrates the identity.

**Claim 2.4** (Cancellation)**.** _Let x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,p_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>2</sub> _be left variables and y_<sub>1</sub>_,y_<sub>2</sub>_,y_<sub>3</sub>_,q_<sub>1</sub>_,q_<sub>2</sub> _be right variables. Put p_<sub>3</sub>=0 _and q_<sub>3</sub>=-_q_<sub>1</sub>-_q_<sub>2</sub>_. Then_

\(\sum_{j=1}^3[(x_1+p_j)(y_j+q_j)+(x_2-p_j)y_j]-(x_1+x_2)(y_1+y_2+y_3)=p_1q_1+p_2q_2.\) (4)

_Proof._ For each _j_, the expression in brackets is (_x_<sub>1</sub>+_x_<sub>2</sub>)_y<sub>j</sub>+x_<sub>1</sub>_q<sub>j</sub>+p<sub>j</sub>q<sub>j</sub>_. Summing over _j_, the first terms cancel the subtracted product, the second sum to zero because _q_<sub>1</sub>+_q_<sub>2</sub>+_q_<sub>3</sub>=0, and the last sum to _p_<sub>1</sub>_q_<sub>1</sub>+_p_<sub>2</sub>_q_<sub>2</sub> because _p_<sub>3</sub>=0.

Note that the variables _x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_ can be arbitrary: the identity always recovers the same two-term dot product. We will choose them so that the six positive products for different outputs belong to one small collection.

## The shared products.

Fix the integer \(k\ge 2\) from Theorem 2.3 for the rest of this construction. Recall that _R=k_2<sup>_k_-1</sup> and _S_=3<sup>_k_-1</sup>, and let \(U\in\mathbb{Z}^{R\times 2}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{Z}^{2\times S}\). Label the rows of _U_ by (_h,u_), with \(h\in[k]\) and \(u\in\{1,2\}^{k-1}\), and the columns of _V_ by \(v\in\{1,2,3\}^{k-1}\). To match the three values of _j_ in Theorem 2.4, extend the entry notation by

\(U_{(h,u),3}=0,V_{3,v}=-V_{1,v}-V_{2,v}.\)

These are abbreviations for linear forms in the original entries.

For a tuple _a_ of length _k_, write \(a_{-\ell}\) for the tuple obtained by deleting coordinate \(\ell\), keeping the others in their original order. For example, (_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,a_<sub>3</sub>)<sub>-2</sub>=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>3</sub>).

For each \(a\in\{1,2\}^k\) and \(b\in\{1,2,3\}^k\), define

\(A_{a,b}=\sum_{\ell=1}^k(-1)^{a_\ell-1}U_{(\ell,a_{-\ell}),b_\ell},B_{a,b}=\sum_{\ell=1}^k\mathbf{1}_{a_\ell=1}V_{b_\ell,b_{-\ell}}.\) (5)

Here \(\mathbf{1}_{a_\ell=1}\) is 1 if \(a_\ell=1\) and 0 otherwise. Our shared collection consists of the 6_<sup>k</sup>_ products _A<sub>a,b</sub>B<sub>a,b</sub>_. Each multiplies a linear form in _U_ by a linear form in _V_ .

The output ((_h,u),v_) uses the six products whose labels satisfy _a_<sub>-_h_</sub>=_u_ and _b_<sub>-_h_</sub>=_v_. Only the pair (_a<sub>h</sub>,b<sub>h</sub>_) varies, so these labels form a six-point coordinate line. Each label belongs to one such line for each \(h\in[k]\); thus each shared product serves _k_ outputs. Figure 2 illustrates this pattern for _k_=2.

Along this line, the \(\ell=h\) terms in equation (5) supply the entries of the desired dot product. The remaining terms play the roles of _x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_ in Theorem 2.4, so one private product cancels their contribution. We verify this next.

Use the six shared products with labels (_a(i),b(j_)), and put \(p_j=U_{(h,u),j},q_j=V_{j,v}(1\le j\le 3).\) Our extended notation gives _p_3=0 and _q_3=-_q_1-_q_2, as required. ## 2.2 The recursive computation

We now use Theorem 2.3 to reduce the middle dimension of a matrix product by a factor of two. A _subproblem_ consists of two input matrices and a set of entries of their product that we want to compute. The original subproblem is to multiply \(X\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times d}\) by \(Y\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times m}\) at the _w_ specified positions.

We first explain one reduction step, then bound three costs after iterating it: preparing input linear forms, multiplying them, and reconstructing the requested outputs. Padding the input dimensions will then give Theorem 2.1. We first count arithmetic operations on matrix values, and account for request processing and intermediate magnitudes at the end.

### One reduction step.

Fix an integer \(k\ge 2\) and let _R=k_2<sup>_k_-1</sup> and _S_=3<sup>_k_-1</sup>, as in Theorem 2.3.

**Claim 2.5** (One reduction step)**.** _Consider matrices_ \(X\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times D}\) _and_ \(Y\in\mathbb{Z}^{D\times M}\)_, with w distinct specified entries of XY. Suppose R|N, S|M, and_ 2|_D. This subproblem reduces to RS=k_6<sup>_k_-1</sup> _private subproblems and_ 6_<sup>k</sup> shared subproblems. Each multiplies matrices of dimensions_

\(\left(\frac{N}{R}\times\frac{D}{2}\right)\text{\textit{and}}\left(\frac{D}{2}\times\frac{M}{S}\right).\)

_The private subproblems receive w requested entries in total, and the shared subproblems receive at most_ 6_w. Their answers determine the w original entries using at most_ 6_w additions and subtractions._

_Proof._ Partition _X_ into blocks _X<sub>i,t</sub>_, with \(i\in[R]\) and \(t\in\{1,2\}\), each of size \((N/R)\times(D/2)\). Partition _Y_ into blocks _Y<sub>t,j</sub>_, with \(j\in[S]\), each of size \((D/2)\times(M/S)\). The (_i,j_) block of the output is

\((XY)_{i,j}=X_{i,1}Y_{1,j}+X_{i,2}Y_{2,j}.\)

This is the same \(R\times 2\) by \(2\times S\) multiplication as in Theorem 2.3, with matrices in place of scalars. The lemma still applies: its formulas use only linear combinations and products of a left input by a right input, always in that order. It expresses each output block as six shared products minus one private product. Each such product multiplies a linear combination of the _X_ blocks by a linear combination of the _Y_ blocks, giving the stated dimensions.

To request an entry of _XY_ , locate its output block (_i,j_) and its position within that block. Request that same position in the six shared products and the one private product used by this block. The seven returned values recover the original entry with five additions and one subtraction.

Each child maintains a set of requested positions, so repeated requests are computed only once. Each output block has its own private product, so the _w_ distinct original requests give exactly _w_ distinct private requests. The original requests also generate 6_w_ shared requests, so the shared children have at most 6_w_ distinct requests in total.

## The bounds after t steps.

For fixed _k_, iterating the rule _t_ times gives the basic dimensions \(R^t\times 2^t\) and \(2^t\times S^t\). We also allow multiples of the outer dimensions, so that arbitrary inputs can be handled by padding. We iterate the input preparation and output reconstruction steps shown in Figure 3.

**Lemma 2.6** (Iterated multiplication rule)**.** _Fix_ \(k\ge 81\)_, with R,S as above. For integers_ \(t\ge 0\) _and_ \(a,b\ge 1\)_, write_<tbc>

\(N=aR^t,D=2^t,M=bS^t.\)

<tbc>_For_ \(0\le j\le t\)_, define the capped request count_

\(B_j=\sum_{s=0}^j\genfrac(){pt}{2}{j}{s}6^smin\left\{w,\frac{NM}{k^s}\right\}.\) (6)

_Given matrices_ \(U\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times D}\) _and_ \(V\in\mathbb{Z}^{D\times M}\)_, any_ \(w\ge 1\) _distinct specified entries of UV can be computed with the following operation bounds:_

1. **_Input preparation:_** _D_<sup>3_k_</sup>(_N+M_) _additions and subtractions to prepare linear forms separately in U and in V._<tbc>

2. **_Scalar multiplication:_** _B<sub>t</sub> multiplications of a prepared form in U by one in V._<tbc>

_3._ **_Output reconstruction:_** _O(tB<sub>t</sub>_) _additions and subtractions to recover the requested entries._

_The algorithm generates O(tB<sub>t</sub>_) _request records._

_Proof._ Apply Theorem 2.5 recursively for _t_ steps. Each step has _T=RS_+6_<sup>k</sup>_=(_k_+6)6<sup>_k_-1</sup> child products, so the full recursion has _T<sup>t</sup>_ leaves, each an \(a\times 1\) by \(1\times b\) outer product. We compute the _a_ left input values and _b_ right input values at every leaf, whether or not that leaf receives requests. We then multiply only the pairs needed for requested leaf entries and reconstruct the requested outputs up the recursion tree.

**Input preparation.** By Theorem 2.3, each entry of a child’s left input matrix is a sum of at most 6_k_ signed entries of its parent’s left input matrix. The same holds for the right input matrices. Substituting these expressions through all _t_ levels writes each left input value at a leaf as a sum of<tbc>

at most (6_k)<sup>t</sup>_ signed entries of the original matrix _U_, and each right input value as such a sum of entries of _V_ . There are _a+b_ input values per leaf. Computing these sums directly from the original inputs uses at most

\(T^t(a+b)(6k)^t\le D^{3k}(a+b)\le D^{3k}(N+M)\)

additions and subtractions, since \(6kT\le 2^{3k}\) for \(k\ge 81\) and _D_=2_<sup>t</sup>_.

**Requested computations.** A request specifies one entry of the output matrix of one subproblem. Starting with the _w_ specified entries of _UV_ , we pass requests down the recursion tree. Each request generates one request in a private child and six requests in shared children, all at the same local position. Requests for the same entry of the same child are merged. Let _Q<sub>j</sub>_ be the total number of distinct requests at depth _j_, counting requests in different subproblems separately. We will show that \(Q_j\le B_j\).

Group the subproblems at depth _j_ by their pattern of shared and private steps from the root. A pattern specifies the type of child at each step, but not which child is chosen. Fix a pattern with _s_ shared steps and _j-s_ private steps. We bound its requests in two ways:

• _Requests generated._ Each original request has one continuation at a private step and at most six at a shared step. It therefore generates at most 6_<sup>s</sup>_ requests with this pattern, or at most 6_<sup>s</sup>w_ over all original requests.<tbc>

• _Available positions._ The full recursion tree has _RS_ choices of private child and 6_<sup>k</sup>_ choices of shared child at each step. Thus (_RS_)<sup>_j-s_</sup>(6_<sup>k</sup>)<sup>s</sup>_ subproblems have this pattern. Each has an output matrix of size \((N/R^j)\times(M/S^j)\), so their total number of output positions is<tbc>

<tbc>\((RS)^{j-s}(6^k)^s\frac{NM}{(RS)^j}=6^s\frac{NM}{k^s},\)<tbc>

<tbc>using _RS=k_6<sup>_k_-1</sup>. Merging repeated requests caps the number of distinct requests by this number of positions.<tbc>

<tbc>Taking the smaller bound for each pattern, and noting that there are \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{j}{s}\) patterns with _s_ shared steps, gives

\(Q_j\le\sum_{s=0}^j\genfrac(){pt}{2}{j}{s}min\left\{6^sw,6^s\frac{NM}{k^s}\right\}=B_j.\)

At depth _t_, the middle dimension is one, so each requested entry is computed by multiplying two prepared input values. This uses \(Q_t\le B_t\) scalar multiplications. We then work back up the tree: each requested parent entry is the sum of its six shared answers minus its private answer, using six additions or subtractions. Request generation and reconstruction therefore each cost \(O(\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}Q_j)\). Finally, \(B_j\le B_t\) for \(j\le t\), since each coefficient \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{j}{s}\) in equation (6) is nondecreasing in _j_. These two costs are thus _O(tB<sub>t</sub>_).

_Proof of Theorem 2.1._ If _d_=1, then _t_=0 and the sum in equation (2) is _w_, so compute the entries directly. Otherwise, set _D_=2_<sup>t</sup>\<_2_d_. Pad the outer dimensions to the least multiples _N,M_ of _R<sup>t</sup>,S<sup>t</sup>_ that are at least _n,m_, respectively, and pad the middle dimension to _D_. Since \(R,S\le 2^{3k}\) and \(D<2d\le d^2\),

\(max\{R^t,S^t\}\le D^{3k}\le d^{6k}\le min\{n,m\}.\)

<tbc>Hence \(N\le 2n\) and \(M\le 2m\). Apply Theorem 2.6. Input preparation costs at most 2(_n+m)d_<sup>6_k_</sup>. Since \(NM\le 4nm\), the capped count satisfies

\(B_t=\sum_{s=0}^t\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t}{s}6^smin\left\{w,\frac{NM}{k^s}\right\}\le 4\sum_{s=0}^t\genfrac(){pt}{2}{t}{s}6^smin\left\{w,\frac{nm}{k^s}\right\}.\)

The extra factor _O(t_) for reconstruction and request generation, and the cost of sorting and deduplicating requests, are absorbed by \(\widetilde{O}\).

If the input entries have absolute value at most \(L\ge 1\), each preparation or reconstruction step combines _O(k_) values. All intermediate values are therefore bounded by (6_k_)<sup>_O(t_)</sup>_L_<sup>2</sup>. Since _k_ is fixed, _t=O_(log_d_), and _L_ is polynomially bounded, these integers have _O_(log(_n+m_)) bits. This proves equation (2).

## 3 Applications to fine grained algorithms

Fine grained algorithms seek to improve the exponent in a problem’s running time. Here our goal is to go below quadratic time for integer 3SUM and below cubic time for APSP. We do this through a convenient intermediate problem, Offline Set Disjointness, which asks whether specified pairs of sets intersect.

This problem connects directly to our matrix multiplication algorithm: the product of two incidence matrices records the intersection sizes, and we only need the entries corresponding to the queried pairs. Known reductions then turn a faster algorithm for this intermediate problem into faster algorithms for 3SUM and APSP. We first give the set-disjointness algorithm, then apply these reductions.

### 3.1 Offline Set Disjointness

An instance of the _Offline Set Disjointness_ problem consists of two families \(S_1,\dots,S_n,T_1,\dots,T_n\subseteq[d]\) and a set \(W\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) of _w_ requested pairs. For each \((i,j)\in W\), we must determine whether \(S_i\cap T_j=\varnothing\).

**Lemma 3.1.** _There is an absolute integer_ \(K\ge 2\) _such that, whenever_ \(d^K\le n\) _and_ \(w\le n^2/\sqrt{d}\)_, Offline Set Disjointness can be solved deterministically in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^2/d^{1/8})\).

_Proof._ Take \(\tau=1/8\) in Theorem 1.1, and set \(K=\kappa(1/8)+1\). Form the incidence matrices \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n\times d}\) and \(Y\in\{0,1\}^{d\times n}\). Since \((XY)_{ij}=|S_i\cap T_j|\), it suffices to compute the entries indexed by _W_. The theorem gives running time

\(\widetilde{O}(nd^{K-1}+nd^{1/8}\sqrt{w})\le\widetilde{O}(n^2/d+n^2/d^{1/8})=\widetilde{O}(n^2/d^{1/8}).\)

Forming the incidence matrices and reading the queries costs _O(nd+w_), which is absorbed by this bound.

### 3.2 Known reductions

To identify the offline set disjointness problem with its graph formulation, use one vertex for each _S<sub>i</sub>_, one for each _T<sub>j</sub>_, and a middle vertex for each element of \[_d_\]. Join sets to their elements and add an outer edge for every requested pair. That edge lies in a triangle exactly when the two sets are not disjoint. This is the _Lopsided All-Edges Sparse Triangle_ formulation \[6, 1\], with a small middle part.<tbc>

For 3SUM, Fischer, Kaliciak, and Polak \[5\] derandomized the set-disjointness reduction of Kopelowitz, Pettie, and Porat \[4\]. For Exact Triangle, Vassilevska Williams and Xu \[6\] gave a randomized reduction to the lopsided problem. Chan and Xu \[7\] gave a deterministic reduction to All-Edges Sparse Triangle, but its construction does not ensure the small middle part needed here. Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\] obtain the deterministic lopsided reduction by combining deterministic hashing with the earlier graph constructions. We use these reductions as black boxes.

_Proof of Theorem 1.2. 3SUM._ Fischer, Kaliciak, and Polak \[5\] show that, for every fixed \(0<\eta<1\), a deterministic truly subquadratic algorithm for Offline Set Disjointness with _O(n_) sets, universe size \(O(n^{2\eta})\), set size \(O(n^\eta)\), and \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) queries gives a deterministic truly subquadratic algorithm for 3SUM. Choose \(\eta>0\) with \(2\eta K<1\). After padding the families and universe to sizes \(\Theta(n)\) and \(d=\Theta(n^{2\eta})\), respectively, the query bound is \(O(n^2/\sqrt{d})\). A constant number of query batches allows Theorem 3.1 to solve these instances in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\eta/4})\) time, giving the 3SUM conclusion.

_APSP._ Exact Triangle asks whether an integer-weighted tripartite graph with _n_ vertices per part contains a triangle whose edge weights sum to zero. We restrict to weights of magnitude _n_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>. Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1\] reduce it deterministically, for \(16\le d\le n\) and an integer \(1\le g\le\sqrt{d}\), to _O(ng_) set-disjointness instances with parameters (_n,d_) and at most \(n^2/\sqrt{d}\) queries each, with additional time

\(\widetilde{O}(n^3/g+n^{\omega+o(1)}d^{3/2}+n^2dg),\)

where \(\omega<3\) is the square matrix multiplication exponent.

Choose \(d=\lfloor n^\varepsilon\rfloor\) for a sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and set \(g=\lceil d^{1/16}\rceil\). By Theorem 3.1, the oracle calls cost \(\widetilde{O}(ng\cdot n^2/d^{1/8})=\widetilde{O}(n^3/d^{1/16})\), as does the first overhead term. Since \(\omega<3\), choosing \(\varepsilon\) small enough also ensures \(d^K\le n\) and makes the other two overhead terms smaller than this bound. Thus Exact Triangle takes \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3-\rho})\) time for some constant \(\rho>0\).

The deterministic reduction of Vassilevska Williams and Williams \[8, 9\] solves APSP in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3-\rho/3})\) time, using only the decision version of Exact Triangle. Absorbing logarithmic factors gives the claimed polynomial improvement.
